A.name: Letter A
A.description: Both hands form a triangle with the index fingertips and thumbs meeting each other.
A.fingers: Use both hands. Touch the right and left index fingertips and thumbs together until they form a triangle.
A.tip: Make sure the triangle shape is clearly visible to the camera.

B.name: Letter B
B.description: The left hand opens three fingers while the right hand points toward the fingers on the left hand.
B.fingers: Open three fingers on the left hand. Point or touch the right index finger toward the left-hand finger area.
B.tip: Short version: left hand with three fingers open, right index finger touching them.

C.name: Letter C
C.description: One hand forms a C-shaped curve with the fingers and thumb open.
C.fingers: Use one hand. Curve the fingers and thumb into a clear C shape.
C.tip: Keep the curve open so the C shape is easy to recognize.

D.name: Letter D
D.description: The left hand forms a half-circle curve, then the right index finger stands upright and touches it.
D.fingers: Shape the left hand into a curve. Keep the right index finger straight up and attach it to the side of the left-hand shape.
D.tip: Keep the right index finger vertical so the D shape looks firm.

E.name: Letter E
E.description: One hand opens three fingers to the side while the remaining fingers are folded.
E.fingers: Open the three main fingers to the side. Fold the other fingers so the E silhouette is clearer.
E.tip: Short version: three fingers open to the side while the others stay folded.

F.name: Letter F
F.description: Two fingers on the upper hand open sideways while the lower index finger touches underneath.
F.fingers: Form two upper fingers open to the side. Touch the lower index finger to the bottom of that shape.

G.name: Letter G
G.description: Both hands make fists, one above and one below, facing each other.
G.fingers: Use both hands in fists. Place one hand above and one below so they face each other.

H.name: Letter H
H.description: Both hands have upright index fingers, with one middle finger crossing through the center.
H.fingers: Make two index fingers stand upright. Place one middle finger across the center as a connector.
H.tip: Make sure both upright index fingers are clearly visible.
H.variant: Short version: two upright index fingers with a middle finger crossing between them.

I.name: Letter I
I.description: One hand raises the pinky while the other fingers are folded.
I.fingers: Raise the pinky straight upward. Keep the other fingers folded inward.

J.name: Letter J
J.description: One hand makes a fist with the pinky open, then moves in a J-shaped curve.
J.fingers: Make a fist and open the pinky. Move it in a curve that resembles the letter J.
J.tip: Make sure the curved motion is visible in front of the camera.

K.name: Letter K
K.description: One index finger stands upright while the other hand touches its middle with the thumb open to the side.
K.fingers: Keep one index finger upright. Use the other hand to touch the middle of that index finger, with the touching hand thumb open to the side.

L.name: Letter L
L.description: The index finger points up and the thumb opens sideways to form an L angle.
L.fingers: Raise the index finger and open the thumb to the side until they form an angle like the letter L.

M.name: Letter M
M.description: One hand is open while three fingers from the other hand touch the center of the palm.
M.fingers: Open one palm. Place three fingers from the other hand on the center of that palm.

N.name: Letter N
N.description: One palm is open while the index and middle fingers from the other hand touch the center of the palm.
N.fingers: Open one palm facing forward. Place the index and middle fingers from the other hand in the center of the palm.
N.variant: Alternative version: one hand open facing forward, with two fingers from the other hand touching the center of the palm.

O.name: Letter O
O.description: The thumb and index finger form a circle while the other fingers stay open.
O.fingers: Join the thumb and index finger into a circle. Keep the other fingers open.

P.name: Letter P
P.description: One index finger stands upright while the thumb and index finger of the other hand form a curve touching its top.
P.fingers: Keep one index finger upright. Shape the other hand into a curve with the thumb and index finger, then touch the top of the upright index finger.
P.variant: Alternative version: one index finger upright, with the thumb and index finger of the other hand forming a curve that touches its tip.

Q.name: Letter Q
Q.description: The thumb and index finger of one hand form a circle while the other index finger touches underneath.
Q.fingers: Make a circle with the thumb and index finger. Use the other index finger to touch the bottom of the circle.

R.name: Letter R
R.description: One hand has an upright index finger while the middle finger bends and touches the thumb.
R.fingers: Raise the index finger. Bend the middle finger until it touches or rests against the thumb.

S.name: Letter S
S.description: Both hands form curves with the thumb and index finger, with the index fingertips facing each other.
S.fingers: Use both hands. Each hand forms a curve with the thumb and index finger, then the index fingertips face each other.

T.name: Letter T
T.description: One index finger stands upward while the other index finger lies horizontally across its top.
T.fingers: Raise one index finger upward. Place the other index finger horizontally so it touches the top of the first index finger.

U.name: Letter U
U.description: The index finger and pinky open upward while the other fingers are folded.
U.fingers: Open the index finger and pinky upward. Keep the other fingers folded.

V.name: Letter V
V.description: The index and middle fingers open upward to form a V while the other fingers are folded.
V.fingers: Open the index and middle fingers upward until they form the letter V. Fold the other fingers.

W.name: Letter W
W.description: Two index fingers stand upright while both thumbs meet in the center to form two W-like angles.
W.fingers: Use both hands. Raise both index fingers and meet the thumbs in the center until they form two angles like the letter W.

X.name: Letter X
X.description: Both index fingers cross at the center.
X.fingers: Use both index fingers and cross them in the center to form the letter X.

Y.name: Letter Y
Y.description: One hand opens the index finger and thumb into an angle while the other index finger touches its center.
Y.fingers: Open the index finger and thumb of one hand into an angle. Use the other index finger to touch the center of that shape.

Z.name: Letter Z
Z.description: One hand opens horizontally forward with the palm facing down.
Z.fingers: Open one hand horizontally toward the front. Keep the palm facing downward.

howItWorks.title: Browser-native BISINDO recognition, from camera frame to sentence.
howItWorks.lead: A technical but readable tour of how SignifyAI captures camera frames, runs YOLO11n ONNX in the browser, commits stable BISINDO alphabet predictions, and turns confirmed letters into editable text.
howItWorks.faqAnswer: The current production model focuses on BISINDO alphabet recognition from A to Z.

steps.title: Start a local camera session
steps.desc: The workspace requests camera access from the browser and keeps the live video stream inside the active page session.

steps.title: Normalize each frame
steps.desc: A frame is drawn into a 640 x 640 canvas, converted from RGBA image data into an RGB tensor, and passed to the model using the configured ONNX input shape.

steps.title: Run YOLO11n ONNX in the browser
steps.desc: ONNX Runtime Web executes the BISINDO YOLO11n artifact through a worker when possible, falls back to the main thread when needed, and uses WebGPU or WASM depending on browser support.

steps.title: Commit letters into text
steps.desc: The top detection is filtered through confidence thresholds and a small weighted-vote accumulator before confirmed letters are added to the sentence builder, saved as text history, and optionally read aloud.

howItWorks.limitationsTitle: The useful path is narrow on purpose: fast, visible, and bounded.

limitations.title: Alphabet scope

limitations.title: Device conditions matter

limitations.title: Text history, not video storage

research.title: Browser-native BISINDO alphabet recognition in SignifyAI.

about.label: About this research
about.title: Browser AI for BISINDO learning
points: YOLO11n ONNX inference in the browser
BISINDO alphabet detection with visible limits
Accessible learning flows without production FastAPI

blocks.text: SignifyAI is best understood as a browser-native BISINDO alphabet recognition system. It uses the camera to observe hand shapes, runs an ONNX object-detection model locally in the frontend, and converts stable A-Z predictions into editable text.

This distinction matters. The application does not claim full semantic sign-language translation, certified interpretation, or natural-language rewriting. Its production scope is narrower and easier to verify: recognize BISINDO alphabet classes, expose confidence, and help users build a sentence from confirmed letters.

The production architecture is intentionally frontend-first. Camera frames move through preprocessing, ONNX Runtime Web, YOLO postprocessing, and a letter accumulator without calling the legacy FastAPI prediction endpoint.
The research question is therefore practical: how far can a web application go when model execution, interaction feedback, and privacy boundaries are kept close to the user device?

BISINDO learning tools need more than a model score. Users need fast feedback, clear states, and honest boundaries so the interface can support practice without pretending to replace trained interpreters.
Transparent Accessibility
A visible confidence score, camera status, and editable sentence builder help users understand what the system has detected and what still needs human judgment.
Lower Deployment Friction
Running inference in the browser removes a production dependency on a model-serving backend. That makes classroom demos, low-cost pilots, and mobile access easier to reason about.
Learning-Oriented Feedback
The translate and practice surfaces share the same recognition boundary. Translation commits letters into text, while practice asks users to hold a target letter long enough for stable recognition.
Responsible Claims
A scoped alphabet recognizer can still be valuable when the product says exactly what it can and cannot do. Overclaiming would make the tool less safe, not more impressive.
The work is technical, but the product standard is human-centered: keep the loop understandable, recoverable, and respectful of the communities it aims to support.
The production loop is a compact browser inference pipeline. It starts with camera capture and ends with a committed letter, not a hidden server-side translation service.
1. Camera Capture
The browser obtains a live video stream after user permission. During detection, frames are sampled on an interval tuned differently for mobile and desktop devices.
2. Frame Preprocessing
Each frame is drawn into a 640 x 640 canvas. The RGBA pixel buffer is converted into a normalized RGB tensor matching the ONNX model input.
3. YOLO11n ONNX Inference

ONNX Runtime Web loads the BISINDO YOLO11n artifact from the public model path. The runtime tries a worker-backed path first, uses cached model bytes when available, and falls back to main-thread execution if worker inference fails.
4. Detection Decoding
The output tensor is decoded into A-Z detections with bounding boxes and confidence values. Low-confidence candidates are filtered, and class-aware non-maximum suppression keeps the strongest boxes.
5. Letter Commitment

The UI selects the highest-confidence detection and sends it into a letter accumulator. Very high confidence can commit quickly; lower confidence must win a short weighted vote before the letter is added to the sentence.
This keeps the experience responsive while reducing repeated commits from a held gesture. The saved history contains text entries and metadata rather than raw camera video.
SignifyAI combines a Next.js workspace, ONNX Runtime Web, a YOLO11n model artifact, and Supabase-backed user data. The important architectural choice is where inference happens: in the browser.
Model Manifest
The frontend declares a BISINDO model manifest with architecture yolo11n, model file best.onnx, input size 640, confidence threshold 0.5, IoU threshold 0.45, and labels A through Z.
Runtime Execution
ONNX Runtime Web is configured with local WASM assets. If WebGPU is available, the runtime attempts WebGPU with WASM fallback; otherwise it runs with WASM.
Worker and Main-Thread Paths

A worker predictor keeps model execution away from the UI thread when possible. If worker creation or worker inference fails, the application falls back to a main-thread predictor instead of breaking the session.
Caching
The model is requested from the browser using force-cache and the Cache API when available. This reduces repeated model download cost across sessions on supported browsers.
Data Boundary
Supabase supports authentication, history, profile, progress, and preferences. It is not the production model-serving path for translate and practice inference.
This architecture keeps model execution close to the camera session while still allowing user data to sync through the application backend services that are actually needed.

The AI layer in the current production app is an object-detection model, not a general language model. It predicts BISINDO alphabet classes from image frames and returns confidence-scored bounding boxes.
YOLO-style detection is useful here because the UI needs both a class label and spatial evidence that a hand shape is present. The postprocessor decodes the ONNX output into candidate detections.

The model output is not accepted blindly. Detections below the configured confidence threshold are discarded, boxes are clamped to the input image size, and overlapping boxes of the same class are reduced through non-maximum suppression.

Temporal stability is handled at the product layer. The letter accumulator prevents a held sign from being committed repeatedly and uses weighted voting when the prediction is plausible but not high enough for immediate commit.

This design separates model confidence from user-facing commitment. A detection can be visible in the UI before it becomes part of the sentence, which makes the system easier to inspect during testing.

Future model research can still explore stronger architectures or multi-model selection, but the current shipped behavior should be evaluated against the A-Z ONNX contract that exists in the codebase.
That contract is what keeps the product honest: the model recognizes alphabet classes; the interface helps users turn stable detections into text.

Training is outside the live browser session, but the deployed app makes its training assumptions visible. The model artifact is an ONNX export named best.onnx and the active labels are the BISINDO alphabet A-Z.
Dataset Scope

A reliable alphabet recognizer requires examples across signers, hand sizes, skin tones, lighting conditions, camera positions, and backgrounds. Without that diversity, confidence in the browser can look precise while still failing real users.
Annotation Contract
The runtime expects object-detection style outputs: class scores and bounding boxes. That implies training data must be labeled consistently with the A-Z class list and hand-region boxes.
Export Boundary
The deployed artifact is loaded as ONNX in the frontend. Any future training change has to preserve compatible input names, output shapes, image size, labels, and postprocessing expectations.

The repository also keeps legacy and parity-oriented backend tests separate from production inference. Those checks are useful for comparing model artifacts, but they do not make FastAPI a production dependency.
Validation

Validation should include held-out signers, mobile cameras, lower-light environments, and browser runtime checks. Unit tests can prove tensor decoding and state transitions; only device testing can prove real camera behavior.
Continuous Improvement
As more data becomes available, retraining should be paired with regression checks for confidence calibration, false positives, latency, and the weighted-vote thresholds used in the interface.
The goal is not only a higher score; it is a model that remains understandable and usable when embedded in a real browser workflow.
Accuracy in SignifyAI is a combined model and interaction problem. The model can return a class and confidence, but the product decides when that prediction becomes a committed letter.

The first improvement path is dataset quality. More varied examples of each BISINDO alphabet sign reduce the chance that the recognizer only works for a narrow group of users or a single camera setup.

The second path is calibration. Thresholds for confidence, IoU, fast commit, and weighted vote should be measured against false positives, repeated commits, and missed signs rather than tuned by feel.
The third path is runtime measurement. WebGPU, WASM, worker execution, and mobile browsers can produce different latency profiles, so performance should be observed across actual devices.
The fourth path is UX feedback. If the interface shows ready, detecting, confidence, and error states clearly, users can adjust their hand position or lighting before assuming the model is wrong.
A stronger future model should therefore ship with stronger evaluation evidence: signer diversity, device diversity, latency numbers, and documented failure modes.
The current SignifyAI scope fits use cases where alphabet-level recognition, feedback, and practice are useful. It should not be positioned as a replacement for certified interpretation.
Classroom Demonstrations
Teachers can use the browser workspace to demonstrate how camera framing, confidence, and model boundaries affect recognition of BISINDO alphabet signs.
Independent Practice
Learners can practice target letters, hold a sign until it is recognized, and review progress without installing a native application.
Accessibility Prototyping
Teams can evaluate whether browser-based model execution is suitable for low-friction accessibility prototypes before investing in heavier infrastructure.
Research Evaluation
Researchers can inspect how thresholding, postprocessing, and UI commitment rules shape the final user experience beyond raw model output.
Development and Parity Testing
Developers can keep legacy backend parity tests separate while using the browser ONNX path as the production behavior to validate.
These use cases are intentionally bounded. The value comes from making a specific workflow reliable, understandable, and testable.

Research and development should extend SignifyAI without weakening its current boundary. The production path is browser ONNX inference for BISINDO alphabet recognition; future work must preserve that clarity or explicitly document a new scope.
Model Variants
Additional YOLO variants or future architectures can be evaluated behind an explicit model registry and admin or developer controls. Silent backend switching would make results hard to audit.
Dataset Expansion
More diverse BISINDO alphabet data is the most direct path to fairer recognition. Expansion should track signer demographics, device types, lighting, and annotation quality.
Browser Performance
The runtime must be measured on WebGPU and WASM paths, desktop and mobile browsers, and devices with different CPU and GPU capabilities.
Interaction Metrics
Model accuracy should be paired with product metrics such as time to first detection, repeated commit rate, empty-frame recovery, and practice hold success.
Ethical Boundaries
The product should continue to state that it is a learning and communication aid, not a certified interpreter. Community review is essential before broadening claims.
A careful roadmap can improve model quality while keeping the user-facing promise precise and testable.

SignifyAI demonstrates a practical browser-first approach to BISINDO alphabet recognition. The system captures camera frames, runs YOLO11n ONNX locally, decodes detections, and commits stable letters into text.

Its strength is not that it solves all sign-language translation. Its strength is that the implemented boundary is visible: A-Z alphabet classes, confidence-scored detections, browser inference, and editable output.
That boundary makes the product easier to test, easier to explain, and safer to improve. Users can see when the model is confident, when it is uncertain, and when human judgment is still required.
Future work should broaden capability only with matching evaluation evidence, especially across real devices, diverse signers, and community-informed accessibility requirements.
